draft.title: Direct and indirect evaluation
card: Evaluation means judging something as good or bad. Writers can do this in two ways.
The writer states the judgement openly, such as "The council's plan is foolish." The reader is told what to think.
The writer hints at the judgement through comparisons and loaded words. "The council's plan is a sandcastle waiting for the tide" leads the reader to see it as weak without saying so.
A loaded word carries a positive or negative feeling. Calling a speech "rambling" rather than "long" suggests a negative view.
draft.remember: Direct evaluation says the judgement. Indirect evaluation leads you to it.

a.q: Which sentence judges a new bus timetable indirectly?
opts: The timetable is a maze that leaves commuters lost
The timetable is poor and should be scrapped
The timetable is a terrible idea
The timetable is clearly the worst one yet
a.why: The comparison to a maze hints that the timetable is confusing without calling it bad. The other three state the judgement openly with words such as poor, terrible and worst.
a.clue: Which one hints rather than says?

b.q: A reviewer writes: "The film is boring, and I would not recommend it." How does the reviewer judge the film?
opts: Directly, by stating the judgement openly
Indirectly, through hints that lead the reader
Neither, because it is only a personal opinion
b.why: Boring and "would not recommend" state the view outright, so it is direct. Being an opinion does not make it indirect, as evaluation is always a judgement. It has no comparison or hints.
b.clue: Does the reader have to work out the view?

a.best: The timetable is a maze that leaves commuters lost

b.best: Directly, by stating the judgement openly
